summary: Documents the needs of various industries for multi-hop paths with deterministic properties for characterized flows, such as bounded latency. It frames the problem that the Deterministic Networking work addresses. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Some machines, like factory robots, need messages to arrive on time every time. This document explains why ordinary networks that sometimes run late are not good enough for them.

why do industrial networks need bounded latency
what is packet replication elimination and ordering
subtitle: Why some industries need networks that deliver packets on a guaranteed schedule, and what work that implies for the IETF.

tldr.problem: Industrial control, audio and video, and vehicle systems need multi-hop paths with guaranteed latency and ultra-low packet loss, but ordinary packet networks cannot promise that.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC frames the problem: reserve resources before sending, characterize each flow, set up paths centrally (with a PCE) or in a distributed way, and optionally duplicate packets over separate paths.
tldr.outcome: It is a problem statement, not a protocol. It lists what the DetNet work must cover, and it notes that the architecture was written separately.

facts.value: Flows may absorb more than half of capacity

today: RFC 8557 is an Informational RFC from May 2019 and has not been obsoleted or updated. The DetNet Working Group wrote the architecture separately, as a document this RFC refers to by its draft name.

sections.title: Why Deterministic Networking
sections.content:
RFC 8557 is a problem statement for Deterministic Networking (DetNet). It builds on RFC 8578, which shows that many industries beyond industrial automation and control systems have strong and similar needs for network services with latency guarantees and ultra-low packet loss.

As these networks grow and become structured, deterministic forwarding is needed beyond the LAN boundary. The RFC says the convergence of IT and Operation Technology (OT) networks requires Layer 3 as well as Layer 2 capabilities, so the work must not be confined to Ethernet or to IEEE 802.
sections.plainLanguage: Factories and power grids used to use special wires for important messages. Now they want to share normal networks, so the networks must learn to keep their promises about timing.

sections.title: What Applications Need
sections.content:
The goals are to move applications with critical timing and reliability needs off special-purpose fieldbus technologies and onto packet networks, while the same network keeps carrying ordinary statistically multiplexed traffic. RFC 8578 lists the features such applications need:

  • Time synchronization of all hosts and network nodes, accurate to between 10 nanoseconds and 10 microseconds depending on the application.
  • Deterministic flows, unicast or multicast, with absolute guarantees of minimum and maximum end-to-end latency, sometimes tight jitter, and a packet loss ratio in the range of 10^-9 to 10^-12 or better on Ethernet.
  • Flows that can absorb more than half of the available bandwidth, so massive over-provisioning is ruled out.
  • Scheduling, shaping and limiting of critical packets at each hop.
  • Defenses against misbehaving hosts, routers or bridges, and methods for reserving resources.

The RFC states that reserving resources before packet transmission is the one fundamental shift in application behavior that cannot be avoided. A network cannot deliver finite latency and practically zero loss to an arbitrarily high offered load, and zero loss for unthrottled flows needs buffers dedicated to specific flows or classes of flows.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like booking a seat on a train before you travel instead of just turning up. Without a booked seat, nobody can promise you will arrive on time.

sections.title: The Problem Areas
sections.content:
Section 3 lists the open problems. For topologies, the deterministic path may run end to end between application hosts, or be a tunnel between an ingress point and an egress router. DetNet does not aim to set up deterministic paths over the global Internet, and the limits of a domain remain unclear. For flow characterization, deterministic forwarding applies only to flows with well-defined characteristics such as periodicity and burstiness, and these must be specified before a path is set up.

For duplicated data, some flows need packet duplication and elimination over non-congruent paths to reach a high enough delivery ratio. The RFC asks for a small number of packet formats and protocols, preferably just one of each, to serialize packets of a stream, replicate them, and discard duplicates. Reusing an existing solution is preferred to inventing a new one.
sections.plainLanguage: Before building the fast lane, you must decide where it goes, what kind of traffic may use it, and how to send spare copies of a message by different roads so one gets through.

sections.title: Setting Up Paths
sections.content:
A centralized model, such as a Path Computation Element (PCE) per RFC 4655, enables global and per-flow optimization. The RFC asks DetNet to describe interaction and data models to report topology and device capabilities, request path setup for a new flow, manage the path life cycle (instantiate, modify, update, delete), adapt to events such as loss of a link, and expose path status to end devices. It also lists Packet Replication, Elimination, and Ordering Functions (PREOF) for reliability and in-band indication of flows and packet sequences.

A distributed alternative without a PCE could build on RSVP-TE (RFC 3209), with neighbor discovery, a DetNet-aware Constrained Shortest Path First calculation, and path installation by an extended control protocol. The RFC says the focus should be to deliver the centralized approach first.
sections.plainLanguage: One way is to have a single traffic controller plan every road. Another is for the cars to work out the route between themselves. The document says to do the traffic-controller version first.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
For DetNet, the time of delivery can matter as much as the contents of a packet. A man-in-the-middle attacker can add and adjust delays on a link and disrupt a real-time application without breaking any encryption (see RFC 7384).

Control networks today rely on physical isolation. DetNet virtualizes them over a converged IT/OT infrastructure, which adds the risk of flows interfering as they share resources. The requirement is that there is no possible data leak from or into a deterministic flow. Overall security must cover protection of signaling, authentication and authorization of controlling nodes, identification and shaping of flows, and isolation of flows.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone just makes your message a little late, a robot arm may swing at the wrong moment. So the network must also keep each reserved lane private and safe from interference.
